title: Management of people, stock on hand and costs of a poultry farming unit, at

lessons.title: Managing people in a poultry unit
lessons.html:
People drive performance

Two poultry houses with the same equipment and genetics can perform very differently because of the people who run them. As unit manager, you are responsible for staffing levels, skills, performance, discipline and wellbeing, within South African labour law.

Staffing and structure

Work out labour needs from the production plan: number of houses, bird type, level of automation and peak tasks such as placement, vaccination, catching and clean-out. Define clear roles, for example house attendant, team leader, maintenance hand and store clerk, each with a written job description. Avoid relying on one person for critical knowledge; cross-train so that leave and illness do not stop production.

Legal framework

Employment must comply with the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 and the applicable minimum wage and farm worker provisions, the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 for fair discipline and dismissal, the Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998 and the OHS Act 85 of 1993. Contracts, working hours, overtime, leave and payslips must be in order. Get advice from a labour consultant or your company HR when in doubt.

Performance management

  • Set measurable targets linked to production, such as mortality, records completed, biosecurity audit scores.
  • Give regular feedback, not only at annual reviews.
  • Recognise good performance; some farms use production bonuses tied to flock results.
  • Identify training needs and arrange skills programmes and learnerships.

Discipline and grievances

Have a written disciplinary code and grievance procedure that staff know. Investigate the facts, give the employee a chance to respond and apply sanctions consistently. Keep records of every step.

Wellbeing and communication

Hold regular team meetings. Provide clean change rooms, toilets and eating areas. Poultry work is dusty and repetitive, so rotate tasks where possible, and make sure PPE is supplied and replaced.

lessons.title: Controlling stock on hand
lessons.html:
Stock is money on the shelf

A poultry unit holds large amounts of stock: feed in silos and bags, vaccines and medicines, disinfectants, litter material, gas, diesel, spares, packaging and the birds themselves. Poor stock control leads to shortages that hurt birds, waste through expiry or spoilage, and theft.

Setting stock levels

For each item decide a minimum level, reorder point and maximum level based on daily use and supplier lead time. Example: if a site uses 8 tonnes of feed a day and the mill needs two days' notice, the reorder point must cover at least two days plus a safety margin. Do not overstock perishable items such as vaccines or feed that can go stale or mouldy.

Controls

  • A single responsible storekeeper with locked stores.
  • Issue only against a signed requisition.
  • Stock cards or a stock system updated on every movement.
  • First expired, first out (FEFO) for vaccines, medicines and chemicals.
  • Monthly physical counts and investigation of variances.
  • Silo levels reconciled against deliveries and calculated consumption.

Livestock as stock

The birds are the most valuable stock on the farm. Reconcile bird numbers: placed minus mortality minus culls must equal birds on hand. At depletion, birds counted onto trucks must match the expected number. Large unexplained differences suggest recording errors or theft and must be investigated.

Storage conditions

Store feed dry, off the floor and protected from rodents. Store chemicals in a locked, ventilated store away from feed and water, with the safety data sheets available. Keep vaccines in a fridge with a thermometer and a daily temperature log. Store diesel and gas according to the supplier's and fire safety requirements.

lessons.title: Managing costs and budgets
lessons.html:
Knowing your cost of production

Margins in poultry are thin, and feed is usually the biggest single cost. A manager who knows the cost per kilogram of live weight or per dozen eggs can make better decisions about feed, labour, energy and capital spending.

Main cost categories

CategoryExamples
VariableChicks or pullets, feed, vaccines and medicines, litter, gas, electricity, packaging
LabourWages, overtime, bonuses, PPE, training
FixedDepreciation, insurance, rates, finance costs, permanent salaries
MaintenanceRepairs, spares, contractor call-outs

Budgeting

Build a budget per flock and per year from the production plan: birds placed, expected liveability and weights or egg numbers, and feed use from the breed standard and your own history. Price inputs from current quotes in rand. The budget sets the target cost per unit of output.

Monitoring actual costs

Each month, compare actual spending with the budget. Explain big variances. For example, feed cost was over budget because FCR worsened during a heat wave, or electricity rose because the generator ran more during load shedding. Separate price variances, where inputs cost more, from usage variances, where more was used.

Controlling costs without hurting birds

  • Reduce feed waste: correct feeder height, fix spills, control rodents.
  • Improve FCR through good brooding, ventilation and health.
  • Use energy efficiently: maintain fans, insulate, consider solar.
  • Plan maintenance to prevent costly breakdowns.
  • Negotiate supplier prices and compare quotes.

Never cut costs in ways that compromise welfare, biosecurity or food safety; the losses from disease or a failed audit are far larger.

Key points

  • Plan staffing from the production plan and comply with labour law.
  • Set targets, give feedback and apply discipline fairly and consistently.
  • Control stock with set levels, locked stores, FEFO and monthly counts.
  • Reconcile bird numbers from placement to depletion.
  • Budget per flock and explain variances between price and usage.
